title: Understanding Market Participation
hook: Clear Pressure Reader, pass the Knowledge Check, save your Check-In, then pass the Phase 3 Final to complete Reading Price Like a Pro.

questionBank.question: What does a potential demand zone tell you?
options: Price previously left that area strongly upward
Price will bounce there next time

questionBank.question: Price returns to a demand zone. What happens next?
questionBank.why: The zone doesn’t decide what happens now.

questionBank.question: Candles keep closing near their highs. Best read?
options: Buyers appear more aggressive right now

questionBank.question: Long wicks both ways, closes all over the place. Who appears more aggressive?
One huge red candle prints. Who caused it?
options: The chart alone can’t tell us
questionBank.why: Describe what price did before deciding who did it.

questionBank.question: Price is still inside a sideways range. What can you claim?
questionBank.why: A label becomes useful after structure confirms it.

questionBank.question: Which question is most useful to ask a price chart?
options: Did price close back below the level, and is it holding?
How many buy orders were filled?
questionBank.why: Ask what the chart can answer.

questionBank.question: Which of these can a price chart answer?
options: Whether price held above a level

questionBank.question: “The banks are hunting stops today.” What is it?
questionBank.why: Identity and intent aren’t on the chart.

questionBank.question: “Sellers appear more aggressive right now.” What is it?
questionBank.why: A hedged read of the evidence.

questionBank.question: You turn on every layer at once. What should you do?
options: Keep only the layer that answers your question
questionBank.why: Context gets deeper. The chart doesn’t need to get messier.

questionBank.question: The Market Read shows supportive context everywhere. Execution?
options: Still decided by the entry model alone
questionBank.why: A read is not a signal generator.

questionBank.question: Does a Dayli ICC entry now need supply & demand, pressure and accumulation?
“Context > confluence” means…
options: Context helps you understand; it doesn’t add entry rules
questionBank.why: Your chart gets clearer, not your rules heavier.

final.title: Reading Price Like a Pro: Final Gate
intro: This is the mastery gate for all of Phase 3: liquidity, price delivery and participation.
Some scenarios include concepts that don’t matter to the question. Spotting that is part of the test. 17 questions, 80% to pass, unlimited retries with a fresh set.

bank.prompt: Where does buy-side liquidity commonly sit, and what does it tell you about where price goes next?

options.label: Above highs. Nothing guaranteed about where price goes
options.why: It names orders, not a destination.

options.label: Above highs. Price must go take it

bank.prompt: You spot equal highs at the top of a range. Best conclusion?
Inside a defined range, price trades above an internal high. The external high is untouched. Which liquidity was taken?
Bearish structure. Price wicks above a minor high and closes back below. The relevant lower high is untouched. MSS?

options.label: No. MSS needs a close through the relevant swing

bank.prompt: A move travels in three big one-way candles with little overlap. There’s also an FVG on the chart from last week. What describes the move?

options.label: Displaced delivery
options.why: The old FVG is irrelevant to this question.

options.label: A must-fill setup from last week’s FVG
options.feedback: That FVG doesn’t answer this question.

options.label: The gap between candle 1’s low and candle 3’s high

bank.prompt: An FVG formed last month, far from price, and was traded through. Does it matter to today’s question?
Price returns to a potential demand zone. What can you claim?

options.label: Who appears more aggressive right now

bank.prompt: A range forms after a decline. Twitter says accumulation. What can you claim?
“They faked the breakout to trap longs.” Make it objective.

options.label: Price closed above the high, then closed back below it

bank.prompt: Structure bullish, sweep, displacement, FVG, buyers aggressive. The Dayli ICC sequence is incomplete. Entry status?

options.label: WAIT
options.why: Context is supportive. The sequence isn’t complete.

bank.prompt: A valid Dayli ICC sequence forms with no FVG and no sweep. Valid?

options.label: Yes. Neither is required
options.why: We don’t force the method to fit another concept.

bank.prompt: Your friend says: “Price swept liquidity and left an FVG, so I’m entering.” What would you ask her?
bank.model: Whether the Dayli ICC sequence has actually formed. A sweep and an FVG are context. What is the structure doing, and where would she be wrong? Liquidity and FVGs are never required, and they never replace the entry model.

bank.prompt: “This is definitely institutional accumulation.” Rewrite it so it only says what the chart can prove.
bank.model: Price is consolidating between similar highs and lows. I can’t prove who is trading, and the label “accumulation” only becomes useful if structure confirms it with a break and build higher.

reflection.heading: YOU LEARNED MORE WITHOUT MAKING YOUR CHART MESSIER.
reflection.intro:
What you can do now
  • ✓ Locate buy-side and sell-side liquidity
  • ✓ Spot pools, equal highs and equal lows
  • ✓ Separate internal from external liquidity
  • ✓ Describe sweeps without the story
  • ✓ Tell a sweep from a structural break
  • ✓ See how price delivered
  • ✓ Find imbalance and build FVGs
  • ✓ Decide when an FVG matters
  • ✓ Read supply, demand and pressure honestly
  • ✓ Treat accumulation as a hindsight label
  • ✓ Separate evidence from story
  • ✓ Hold it all in a Market Read
MOST IMPORTANTLY… you know the difference between KNOWING A CONCEPT and TRADING A CONCEPT.

pressure-equals-direction.text: Pressure keeps turning into a prediction in your answers. Who appears aggressive right now isn’t who wins.
pressure-equals-direction.label: Buying vs Selling Pressure

supply-demand-guarantee.text: Zones are reading as promises. They show where participation appeared before, not what happens next.
supply-demand-guarantee.label: Supply & Demand Basics

consolidation-equals-accumulation.text: You’re labeling ranges as accumulation before structure confirms the story.
consolidation-equals-accumulation.label: Accumulation & Distribution

participant-identity-assumption.text: You’re naming who traded. The chart can only show what price did.
participant-identity-assumption.label: Aggressive Participation

storytelling-over-evidence.text: Stories are slipping in ahead of evidence. Point at it on the chart first.
storytelling-over-evidence.label: What Price Cannot Prove

context-equals-entry.text: Context keeps turning into entries. Literacy isn’t execution.
context-equals-entry.label: How This Fits Into Dayli ICC

concept-overload.text: More concepts are turning into more rules. Your chart should get clearer, not heavier.
concept-overload.label: How This Fits Into Dayli ICC

fvg-required.text: FVGs are showing up as requirements. Dayli ICC never needs one.
fvg-required.label: FVGs in the Dayli ICC Framework

fvg-must-fill.text: You’re expecting gaps to fill. A revisit is possible, never guaranteed.
fvg-must-fill.label: Why Price May Revisit an Imbalance

liquidity-required.text: Liquidity is showing up as a requirement. It’s context only.
liquidity-required.label: Liquidity in the Dayli ICC Framework

structure-hierarchy-error.text: Context is overriding structure in some reads. Structure first.
structure-hierarchy-error.label: Efficient vs Inefficient

sweep-equals-reversal.text: Sweeps are reading as reversals. A sweep is context, not a turn.
sweep-equals-reversal.label: Liquidity Sweeps

sweep-equals-mss.text: Taking liquidity is reading as an MSS. Ask the structure question separately.
sweep-equals-mss.label: Sweep vs Structural Break

liquidity-as-destination.text: Liquidity is reading as a destination. It describes where orders may rest.
liquidity-as-destination.label: Buy-Side & Sell-Side
